youtube.title: Angles for Kids: Acute, Right, Obtuse and How to Use a Protractor | Grade 4 Math | Toy Box Friends
youtube.description:
Robo thinks the angle with the longest arms is the biggest. Owl tests it, and finds an angle measures turn, not arm length!
Kids learn lines, rays, segments and the vertex; quarter, half and full turns (90°, 180°, 360°) with a door, a clock and Bunny's skateboard; how to sort acute, right, obtuse and straight angles; how to use a protractor (centre, 0 line, count up from 0) with a sense check; adding angles and finding a missing angle; and parallel, perpendicular and intersecting lines.
Try at home: fold paper in half twice to make a right angle tester and hunt for angles. If you test a door, keep fingers away from the hinge and let a grown-up swing it.

objects.text:
An angle is an amount of turn.
90° is a quarter turn, 180° a half turn, 360° a full turn.
Protractor: count up from 0 on your ray.
Sense check: smaller than a corner? Less than 90°.
Fold any paper in half, then in half again. The folded corner is a right angle tester. Hunt for angles: acute, right or obtuse?

do.text: Angle Explorers
Two angles. Easy! The one with the long arms is the bigger angle.
Are you sure? Which angle is bigger? Make your guess.
Which is bigger?
Let's test it. I'll slide the small one on top.
Whoa. The arms line up exactly. It's the same angle!
So arm length does not decide. What does an angle measure?
First, some parts. A line goes on forever, both ways. See the two arrows?
A ray has one endpoint, and goes on forever one way.
A line segment has two endpoints. It stops at both ends.
Two rays that share an endpoint make an angle.
The shared point is called the vertex.
Now let's stretch the arms longer.
Still fifty degrees. Now shorter.
Still fifty degrees! The arms changed, but the turn did not.
angle = amount of turn
An angle is a turn. Watch the door open a quarter turn.
A quarter turn is ninety degrees. That's a right angle.
quarter turn = 90°
The minute hand turns too. From twelve to three is a quarter turn.
From twelve to six is a half turn. One hundred eighty degrees.
All the way round is a full turn. Three hundred sixty degrees.
Fun fact: the 360 comes from ancient Babylon, where people counted in sixties.
Watch me skate! A quarter turn!
A half turn! Skaters call it a one-eighty.
And a full turn, a three-sixty! Back where I started.
Skaters name their tricks by the angle they turn!
A full turn is cut into three hundred sixty tiny equal turns. Each one is one degree.
1° = 1/360 of a turn
One degree is tiny! Ninety of them make a right angle.
Let's sort angles. Our corner tester is the corner of a sheet of paper.
It's a right angle.
Put the corner on the vertex. Is the angle smaller, the same, or bigger?
40 degrees: smaller than the corner. Acute!
90 degrees: it matches the corner. Right!
135 degrees: bigger than the corner. Obtuse!
180 degrees: flat as a line. Straight!
75 degrees: smaller than the corner. Acute!
110 degrees: bigger than the corner. Obtuse!
Here they all are, sorted by their turn.
Does a right angle have to point right? Let's turn it upside down.
Still a square corner. Still ninety degrees. Right just means a square corner.
This is a protractor. It measures angles in degrees. It has two scales.
Step one: put the centre mark on the vertex.
1. centre mark on the vertex
Step two: line up the zero line with one ray.
2. zero line on one ray
Step three: start at the zero on that ray, and count up to the other ray.
3. count up from that zero
My turn! The ray crosses one hundred twenty. So it's one hundred twenty degrees!
Sense check first. Is this angle smaller than a corner?
Yes! So it must be less than ninety. Robo read the wrong scale.
Our ray starts at the zero on the right, so we read the blue scale. Sixty degrees.
Got it. Count from the zero on my ray, then do a sense check.
Now try this one.
Zero, ten, twenty, thirty, forty. Forty degrees, and it is acute.
And this one?
Past ninety, not flat. One hundred thirty five degrees. Obtuse!
Angles add up, like pizza slices. Thirty degrees and sixty degrees.
Slide them together, side by side.
Thirty plus sixty is ninety. A right angle!
A right angle is split by a ray.
One part is thirty five degrees. What is the other part?
Ninety take away thirty five is fifty five degrees.
A straight angle is one hundred eighty.
If one part is one hundred thirty, the other is fifty.
Train tracks are parallel lines. They stay the same distance apart and never meet.
These lines meet at a right angle, like the letter T. They are perpendicular.
Window frames have perpendicular lines too.
These lines cross, but not at a right angle. They are intersecting lines.
parallel · perpendicular · intersecting
Tiny turn is acute!
A corner's right!
Wide is obtuse!
Flat is straight, hold it tight!
Quarter turn?
Quarter turn?
Ninety degrees!
Half turn?
Half turn?
One-eighty!
Angle hunt! The clock is only a turning tool today. Look at the angle between the hands.
What angle do the hands make at three o'clock?
Three o'clock. The hands make a right angle, ninety degrees.
Now one o'clock. What kind of angle?
One o'clock. A small turn: acute, thirty degrees.
Now five o'clock. What kind of angle?
Five o'clock. Wider than a corner: obtuse, one hundred fifty degrees.
Now six o'clock. What kind of angle?
Six o'clock. The hands make a straight line: one hundred eighty degrees.
Letters have angles too. What about V and L?
V is acute. L is a right angle!
Bonus fact: the corners inside a honeycomb cell are one hundred twenty degrees. Obtuse!
Quiz time! One: does making the arms longer make the angle bigger?
No! The turn is the same, so the angle is the same.
Two: a clock shows three o'clock. What kind of angle do the hands make?
A right angle. Ninety degrees.
Three: an angle is one hundred thirty degrees. Acute, right or obtuse?
Obtuse. It's between ninety and one hundred eighty.
Four: a right angle is split into fifty degrees and what?
Forty degrees. Ninety take away fifty is forty.
An angle is an amount of turn.
